To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
AgNO3 and other sulfhydryl-oxidizing agents (e.g., diamide, 4-CMC) induce Ca2+release from skeletal muscle by oxidizing sulfhydryl residues in both the Ca2+release channel and the SR Ca2+-ATPaSe.
AgNO3 and other oxidants cause Ca2+ release in skeletal muscle by oxidizing the Ca2+ binding sites on the CRC and/or the Ca2+-binding sites on the Ca2+-pump.
AgNO3 induces Ca2+ from SR by acting on both SR Ca2+ release channels and SR Ca2+-ATPsase.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of Ca2+ regulation in muscle.
the effects of silver on the SR Ca2+ release system and the possible mechanisms involved.
the effects of Ag+ on the Ca2+-transport system of skeletal muscle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CRC is more sensitive than the Ca2+-pump to the oxidizing effects of AgNO.
AgNO3 induces a biphasical Ca2+ release in SR vesicles by acting on the CRC and Ca2+-ATPaase.
AgNO3 induces Ca2+ efflux from muscle by acting on both SR Ca2+ channels and the Ca2+/ATPase pump.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AgNO3 acts on the CRC to cause Ca2+ release, whereas 4-CMC acts on the CRC alone to induce Ca2+ efflux.
AgNO3 induces a biphasically Ca2+ release in vitro from the SR by acting on the CRC and Ca2+-ATPaSe.

AgNO3 induces Ca2+release from SR in vitro by oxidizing critical sulfhydril groups in the CRC, causing the channel to be constitutively open, and by oxidizing critical sulhydryl groups of the Ca2+- ATPase, causing it to be inhibited.

AgNO3 acts on the Ca2+-transporting proteins to induce a biphasic release of Ca2+ in a manner similar to 4-CMC.
